chapter: Parade of June 1986 and Young Tuxedo today
title: Greg Stafford and Barry Wratten on tradition
summary: Stafford gave Wood a ride and objected to a non-New Orleanian speaking authoritatively about the tradition; he said the music must grow but stay in the tradition.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: No, it's a different, you know, it's, actually Greg Stafford who ended up giving me a ride from that, where that parade ended up, back down to the French market where he was late playing his gig at the Cafe Mediterranean. And I got into that because he had seen me before the parade started talking to, to Barry Ratton. And he had overheard some things that, that Ratton was saying to me, I guess was in response to a question I had asked him about the band that I had heard him play with the week before. And, you know, Greg took a little offense at some, not, I don't know that he knew exactly what Ratton was saying, but what he was taking offense at was Ratton as somebody who was not a New Orleanian being authoritative in telling people about what New Orleanian music was really like when he is not himself of the tradition. I was surprised that Greg was as sensitive about that as he seems to be. And so, you know, he was saying, you know, we don't sound like John Casimir's band sounded like, but, you know, we're, it's 30 years later and everything moves and changes. We shouldn't sound like it. We grow, everybody grows. It's not the same world.

But it's the same tradition. That's basically what he was saying. And I have no real argument with that. You don't want it to be just an antique replica of something else. It's got to be something that's his and of the present. But he was very conscious, and he could articulate that concept, I thought, very well.
